questions.q: What does "knowledge scoping" refer to in a penetration test?
options: The decision of how much information — source code, credentials, network maps — the tester starts the engagement with
The physical size of the building being tested
The number of testers assigned to the engagement
The dollar amount budgeted for the engagement
questions.explain: Knowledge scoping is a separate axis from which systems are in bounds — it's the agreed-upon decision of how much information the tester begins with, which fundamentally changes what the test measures.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff of white-box testing, where the tester starts with full source code, architecture diagrams, and credentials?
options: It is the cheapest option because no reconnaissance is required at all
It always takes longer than black-box testing to complete
It achieves fast, thorough coverage but is the least realistic simulation of an actual external attacker
It cannot legally be performed without a government permit
questions.explain: Full internal knowledge lets a white-box tester move straight to reviewing known logic, making it fast and thorough — but a real external attacker almost never starts with your source code and valid credentials.

questions.q: Why is black-box testing considered the most realistic simulation of an external attacker, and what is its main risk?
options: It starts with zero prior knowledge like a real outside attacker, but risks running out of engagement time before covering everything
It is risk-free because the tester already has full credentials
It is the fastest testing model because no reconnaissance is needed
It is only used for internal employees, never external attackers
questions.explain: A black-box tester starts with nothing beyond perhaps a company name or URL, mirroring a genuine outside attacker — but time spent on reconnaissance and enumeration can mean running out of hours before full coverage is reached.

questions.q: Why does gray-box testing end up being the most common choice for real-world engagements rather than either extreme?
options: It is required by law in most jurisdictions
It is always the cheapest of the three models regardless of scope

Starting with partial knowledge, such as standard user credentials, realistically mirrors common threats like insiders or compromised accounts while covering more ground than black-box within the same time budget
It eliminates the need for a Rules of Engagement document
questions.explain: Gray-box testing mirrors a genuinely common real-world scenario — an insider or compromised low-privilege account — and because the tester doesn't burn hours on reconnaissance a real attacker in that position wouldn't need either, it covers more ground than black-box within a fixed testing window.

questions.q: When should the choice between white-box, gray-box, and black-box testing be decided?
options: Informally on the first day of testing, by the tester alone
During scoping, written into the scope and ROE before testing begins, alongside in-scope/out-of-scope systems
Only after the final report has already been delivered
It never needs to be decided or documented at all
questions.explain: Which knowledge model to use is a scoping decision made in advance, the same way testing windows and in-scope systems are — deciding it on day one of testing risks an engagement that doesn't answer the question the client actually needed answered.
